hero.headline: 36 dogs rescued from Palm City home face long recovery at Humane Society of Treasure Coast
hero.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is working around the clock to medically groom, bathe and examine 36 Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home, with many suffering from eye and skin infections.
hero.body:
A Palm City woman is in custody on a $270,000 bond after authorities discovered 36 Border Collies living in severe neglect inside her home on Alligator Street, leading to 72 charges of animal cruelty. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the animals were in deplorable conditions. All 36 dogs are now being cared for at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast.

Sarah Fisher, a spokesperson for the organization, described the severity of the animals' condition. The shelter found not only matted and underweight dogs with skin issues, but also glass and metal embedded in their fur. The dogs' tongues were bleeding from them biting their tongues, there was feces in their mouths, and their tails might be falling off, Fisher said. The shaving process can take an hour per dog, and as staff members cut and shave, they are finding lots of pieces of rusted metal, sharp metal, and shards of glass stuck in the dogs' fur.

Fisher said some of the dogs are just laying there and don't know what to do. They don't know to lift their head and don't know how to interact with people, showing they were institutionalized. The case dates back to 2020, when animal services first investigated Paige O'Donnell's home and dogs. Court records show complaints continued through 2022 and 2023, with renewed concerns in 2026 leading to surveillance and multiple attempted inspections. The Humane Society said it could take time before the dogs are ready for foster homes or adoption and is asking for community support to help with the recovery efforts.

cards.headline: Republicans Build 40,000-Vote Lead in Florida Primary as Democrats Turn Out at Higher Rate
cards.teaser: Republicans hold a 40,114-vote lead over Democrats in Florida's primary election with less than a week before Election Day, even as Democrats vote at a signific.
cards.body:
Republicans hold a 40,114-vote lead over Democrats in Florida's primary election with less than a week before Election Day, even as Democrats vote at a significantly higher rate relative to their party registration, according to Fresh Take Florida's statewide turnout tracker.

As of 3:30 p.m. Wednesday, more than 1.3 million Floridians had already voted. Republicans accounted for 585,423 ballots compared with 545,309 Democrats. Another 177,542 ballots came from voters outside the two major parties. Republicans enter this election with a registration advantage of roughly 1.54 million voters, with 5.6 million registered Republicans and 4.06 million Democrats. Democrats still lead in mail ballots, with 409,358 Democrats voting by mail compared with 356,500 Republicans, a Democratic lead of 52,858 ballots. Republicans have overwhelmed that advantage at early voting sites, where 228,923 Republicans have voted early in person compared with 135,951 Democrats, a GOP advantage of 92,972 votes.

When turnout is measured against the size of each party, 13.43 percent of registered Democrats have voted compared with 10.45 percent of registered Republicans, almost a three-percentage-point Democratic advantage. About 10.08 percent of registered Democrats have already voted by mail compared with 6.37 percent of Republicans. Republicans have the edge in early in-person participation, 4.09 percent to 3.35 percent. Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said the political environment is shifting and argued the Republican supermajority in the Legislature is breakable this cycle. Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power said Republicans have taken the vote lead and will not look back, predicting a big vote lead on Election Day.

Florida's primary Election Day is August 18, with the state's mandatory early voting period continuing through Saturday, August 15. Political analyst Susan MacManus said enthusiasm only matters if campaigns can turn it into votes. For Democrats, the challenge is proving that dissatisfaction over affordability and the party in power can translate into enough turnout to overcome Florida's Republican registration advantage. For Republicans, it is showing that their larger voter pool and established turnout operation can dominate when all ballots are counted.

cards.headline: Troopers seek Ford F-150 driver after deadly e-bike hit-and-run in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: A 48-year-old Vero Beach man riding an electric bicycle was killed after being struck by a pickup truck that fled the scene Sunday night in unincorporated India.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office has located the vehicle allegedly involved in a deadly hit-and-run crash that killed a 48-year-old Vero Beach man riding an electric bicycle Sunday night near 8th Street and 14th Avenue. An IRCSO analyst located a vehicle matching the truck's description, including a missing passenger-side mirror, while reviewing leads with the Florida Highway Patrol. Deputies used Flock Safety technology and other investigative resources to identify the vehicle, its license plate and information about the driver.

The crash occurred at about 8:57 p.m. Sunday when the man was riding an e-bike near 8th Street and 14th Avenue. Investigators said a light-colored Ford F-150, believed to be a 2015 to 2020 model, was traveling behind the man in the same lane. As the pickup approached the bicyclist, the driver took evasive action, traveling southwest and partially entering the eastbound lane. However, the driver was unable to avoid the bicyclist, and the right side of the pickup struck him.

The bicyclist was thrown onto the roadway and came to rest in the eastbound lane of 8th Street. FHP said the driver fled the scene without rendering aid or contacting law enforcement. The bicyclist was taken to Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

The information from IRCSO's Real Time Crime Center allowed FHP to locate the vehicle and confirm its connection to the crash. IRCSO has not identified the driver or released the identity of the bicyclist who was killed.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce proposes fines up to $500 per day for chronic noise violators
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce city officials are considering tougher noise enforcement that would allow fines of $250 to $500 per day for chronic violators and let the city place liens on properties
cards.body:
Fort Pierce city officials are considering tougher noise enforcement that would allow fines of $250 to $500 per day for chronic violators and let the city place liens on properties where violations occur. Law enforcement responded to nearly 2,000 noise complaint calls in Fort Pierce between April 1, 2025 and April 30, 2026, with about one in three complaints coming from the same 14 city locations. Half of all calls currently come in Sundays between 10 p.m. and morning hours.

The proposed ordinance amendments would expand police enforcement authority and allow officers to issue citations without warnings when noise is so loud, excessive or disruptive that it constitutes a clear and substantial disturbance or breach of the peace. District 1 Commissioner Arnold Gaines said chronic noise offenders are using loopholes in current ordinances by continuing to offend until they receive three warnings from police, then turning down their music. Proposed changes would define chronic violations as three or more verified noise complaints at the same location within 30 days, or six or more within 90 days.

Under the proposal, officers would give violators five minutes to comply after the first warning. A citation to appear would be issued if the violation continued another five minutes or if it was a third violation. An arrest would be made for a fourth offense or if another five minutes passed without correcting the current violation. Parents and guardians would be made responsible for penalties levied against juvenile offenders.

If an offender fails to follow a compliance plan or new complaints continue, incidents could be treated as a public nuisance referred to the city's Nuisance Abatement Board where daily fines of up to $250 to $500 can be ordered. If fines are not paid, a lien may be placed on the property where the incident occurs and the city can foreclose to collect the lien after three months. City Clerk Linda Cox said recommended ordinance changes require two public hearings once final ordinance language is drafted.

cards.headline: Indian River County school district plans to sell 10 properties across county
cards.teaser: The School District of Indian River County is looking to put around 10 properties on the market for potential buyers. The properties are spread across the county and include four o
cards.body:
The School District of Indian River County is looking to put around 10 properties on the market for potential buyers. The properties are spread across the county and include four older schools, older office buildings, and district-owned land, according to William Dodds, CFO of the School District of Indian River County.

Dodds said the properties are no longer necessary after the district consolidated multiple schools. The district is gauging interest from potential buyers before moving forward, and no decisions have been made yet. Money made from the sale of the properties would go back to the district's capital budget.

Ken Krasnow with Cushman and Wakefield, a real estate company working with the school district to sell the properties, said the buildings vary in condition and potential. Some buildings, like Rosewood Magnet School, could be transformed into medical office or flex space. Larger schools and properties could be redeveloped with commercial or retail space along the front and residential in the back.

Dodds said the district will reexamine interest in the properties and whether they need to be sold around December or January. The school board will have final approval. The capital budget funds would help keep district buildings up and enhance facilities.

cards.headline: Florida Homeowners with Aging Roofs Face Rising Insurance Premiums as Companies Limit Coverage
cards.teaser: Insurance companies increasingly raise premiums on asphalt shingle roofs older than 15 years, while metal roofs receive favorable treatment for their 30-year-plus lifespan.
cards.body:
Florida homeowners insurance premiums largely depend on two critical roof factors: age and materials, according to local insurance experts who say the roof serves as a home's primary defense against weather damage. Insurance companies increasingly raise premiums on asphalt shingle roofs older than 15 years, while metal roofs receive favorable treatment for their 30-year-plus lifespan, according to industry professionals. Homeowners with shingle roofs over 15 years face shrinking insurance options, explained Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth-Rindom Insurance in Stuart.

Asphalt shingles remain Florida's most popular and economical roofing choice, but their vulnerability to heat and wind makes them less attractive to insurers as they age. Companies with the most competitive rates only want roofs under 15 years old, so homeowners with 16-year-old roofs can still have options but are starting to eliminate options for themselves, Wiglesworth said. For homeowners reluctant to replace aging roofs, scheduled endorsements offer partial protection. Under this arrangement, insurers cover only 25 percent of an older roof's value while homeowners self-insure the remaining 75 percent.

Metal roofs cost nearly twice as much as asphalt shingles but offer superior long-term protection and insurance advantages, according to Wiglesworth. Florida's insurance market has seen new companies enter the state, with more insurers willing to cover older homes. His advice for homeowners considering roof replacement: call an agent who can shop multiple carriers and ask what it would save them if they got a new roof, even before they get a new roof.

cards.headline: South Fork High School freshman describes hot, crowded bus ride on first day of school
cards.teaser: A Martin County parent says her daughter came home in tears after her first bus ride home from South Fork High School, describing extreme heat and overcrowding on the bus Monday.
cards.body:
Sherri Lindemann's daughter is a freshman at South Fork High School. Lindemann said she was caught off guard when she learned what had upset her child. Lindemann said her daughter described a miserable experience on the ride. She said the bus was extremely hot with no air or ventilation and that there was overcrowding with four kids to every seat, with everybody sweaty and upset. The bus ride took an hour and 15 minutes to get home.

The Martin County School District said it understands why the experience would be concerning for students and families, especially on the first day of school when routines are new and students are adjusting to the year ahead. The district's Transportation team confirmed that 57 students were on the bus on Monday, which falls within regulation for high school buses, and that no seat had 4 students in it. Staff also confirmed the bus's air conditioning system was operating properly, but the district acknowledged that mid-August heat can make any bus ride feel particularly warm.

Lindemann's concerns come after the school district consolidated 3 school bus routes to make transportation more efficient without impacting students. In a statement, the district said the delays had nothing to do with the consolidation. The district said Transportation staff are closely monitoring ridership and routes as drivers become more familiar with traffic patterns and students become accustomed to safely exiting the bus. Families can track their child's bus through the MyReaxiumApp. Those who need help setting up an account can contact the transportation department at 772-219-1287.

hero.headline: Mets, Tortugas split Saturday doubleheader as Zayas powers Game 1 win
hero.teaser: Julio Zayas hit a go-ahead three-run homer for the second straight day, lifting St. Lucie to a 3-1 win before Daytona answered with a 15-7 victory in Game 2.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie Mets and Daytona Tortugas split a Saturday doubleheader at Clover Park, with the Mets taking the opener 3-1 before Daytona answered with a 15-7 victory in Game 2.

The split left the seven-game series tied 3-3 heading into Sunday’s finale. It was also the second time the teams split a doubleheader during the series after each club won once during Wednesday’s twin bill.

## Zayas delivers another go-ahead home run

Julio Zayas provided the biggest swing for St. Lucie in Game 1, hitting a go-ahead three-run home run in the fourth inning to erase a 1-0 Daytona lead.

The homer came one night after Zayas hit a walk-off home run in the bottom of the ninth inning Friday. Saturday’s blast was his third home run of the series.

St. Lucie’s pitching staff made the lead hold up.

Starter Nate Hall worked the first 1 2/3 innings before Caden Wooster took over. Wooster allowed Daytona’s only run when Arnaldo Lantigua hit a solo home run in the third inning.

Ernesto Mercedes followed with two scoreless innings, allowing four hits while striking out three to earn the win.

Miguel Mijias recorded the final five outs for his fourth save of the season, including a perfect seventh inning to close the game.

The Mets held Daytona to 1-for-8 with runners in scoring position and stranded 10 Tortugas runners.

The performance continued a sharp turnaround for St. Lucie’s pitching staff. From the ninth inning of Thursday’s game through the end of Saturday’s opener, the Mets allowed only one run after Daytona had scored 17 runs over the first eight innings Thursday.

Daytona starter Dusty Revis was charged with the loss despite throwing a six-inning complete game on just 63 pitches. Revis allowed five hits and three earned runs while becoming the first Tortugas pitcher since 2019 to record a complete game.

Elian Peña went 1-for-3 for St. Lucie and extended his hitting streak to 10 games.

## Daytona pulls away in Game 2

The nightcap was a much different game, with Daytona breaking a 6-6 tie during a decisive fifth inning.

Mets newcomer Wilmer Lugo appeared to escape the inning by striking out Henry Hunter looking on a 3-2 pitch. Hunter challenged the call using the ABS system, however, and the ruling was overturned to ball four, loading the bases.

Lugo then walked the next two hitters to force home a pair of runs. After Luis Sotillo entered in relief, a wild pitch allowed Hunter to score and stretched Daytona’s lead to 9-6.

Hunter delivered another major blow in the seventh inning, hitting a grand slam off Sotillo to push the Tortugas ahead 13-6.

For the second time in four games, the Mets eventually turned to Zayas to finish the game on the mound as a position player. He recorded the final four outs, allowing a two-run homer to Drew Davies with two outs in the seventh but no additional damage.

Logan Tanner earned the win for Daytona after throwing two scoreless innings of relief.

St. Lucie still produced several offensive highlights in the loss.

Simon Juan went 2-for-3 with a double and his ninth home run of the season.

Kuhio Aloy, the Mets’ 11th-round draft pick, hit a two-run homer in the third inning to tie the game at 6-6. It was Aloy’s first professional home run.

Lugo took the loss after being charged with three runs on one hit and four walks over 2/3 of an inning.

## Series finale set for Sunday

The Mets fell to 16-24 in the second half and 49-57 overall, while Daytona improved to 25-14 in the second half and 46-60 overall.

St. Lucie and Daytona will decide the series Sunday at Clover Park, with first pitch scheduled for 12:10 p.m.

Sunday is Little League Day. Little leaguers who attend wearing their team jerseys will receive free admission courtesy of Holiday Inn Express.

hero.headline: Republicans Build 40,000-Vote Lead in Florida Primary as Democrats Turn Out at Higher Rate
hero.teaser: Republicans hold a 40,114-vote lead over Democrats in Florida's primary election with less than a week before Election Day, even as Democrats vote at a signific.
hero.body:
Republicans hold a 40,114-vote lead over Democrats in Florida's primary election with less than a week before Election Day, even as Democrats vote at a significantly higher rate relative to their party registration, according to Fresh Take Florida's statewide turnout tracker.

As of 3:30 p.m. Wednesday, more than 1.3 million Floridians had already voted. Republicans accounted for 585,423 ballots compared with 545,309 Democrats. Another 177,542 ballots came from voters outside the two major parties. Republicans enter this election with a registration advantage of roughly 1.54 million voters, with 5.6 million registered Republicans and 4.06 million Democrats. Democrats still lead in mail ballots, with 409,358 Democrats voting by mail compared with 356,500 Republicans, a Democratic lead of 52,858 ballots. Republicans have overwhelmed that advantage at early voting sites, where 228,923 Republicans have voted early in person compared with 135,951 Democrats, a GOP advantage of 92,972 votes.

When turnout is measured against the size of each party, 13.43 percent of registered Democrats have voted compared with 10.45 percent of registered Republicans, almost a three-percentage-point Democratic advantage. About 10.08 percent of registered Democrats have already voted by mail compared with 6.37 percent of Republicans. Republicans have the edge in early in-person participation, 4.09 percent to 3.35 percent. Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said the political environment is shifting and argued the Republican supermajority in the Legislature is breakable this cycle. Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power said Republicans have taken the vote lead and will not look back, predicting a big vote lead on Election Day.

Florida's primary Election Day is August 18, with the state's mandatory early voting period continuing through Saturday, August 15. Political analyst Susan MacManus said enthusiasm only matters if campaigns can turn it into votes. For Democrats, the challenge is proving that dissatisfaction over affordability and the party in power can translate into enough turnout to overcome Florida's Republican registration advantage. For Republicans, it is showing that their larger voter pool and established turnout operation can dominate when all ballots are counted.

cards.headline: Florida Homeowners with Aging Roofs Face Rising Insurance Premiums as Companies Limit Coverage
cards.teaser: Insurance companies increasingly raise premiums on asphalt shingle roofs older than 15 years, while metal roofs receive favorable treatment for their 30-year-plus lifespan.
cards.body:
Florida homeowners insurance premiums largely depend on two critical roof factors: age and materials, according to local insurance experts who say the roof serves as a home's primary defense against weather damage. Insurance companies increasingly raise premiums on asphalt shingle roofs older than 15 years, while metal roofs receive favorable treatment for their 30-year-plus lifespan, according to industry professionals. Homeowners with shingle roofs over 15 years face shrinking insurance options, explained Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth-Rindom Insurance in Stuart.

Asphalt shingles remain Florida's most popular and economical roofing choice, but their vulnerability to heat and wind makes them less attractive to insurers as they age. Companies with the most competitive rates only want roofs under 15 years old, so homeowners with 16-year-old roofs can still have options but are starting to eliminate options for themselves, Wiglesworth said. For homeowners reluctant to replace aging roofs, scheduled endorsements offer partial protection. Under this arrangement, insurers cover only 25 percent of an older roof's value while homeowners self-insure the remaining 75 percent.

Metal roofs cost nearly twice as much as asphalt shingles but offer superior long-term protection and insurance advantages, according to Wiglesworth. Florida's insurance market has seen new companies enter the state, with more insurers willing to cover older homes. His advice for homeowners considering roof replacement: call an agent who can shop multiple carriers and ask what it would save them if they got a new roof, even before they get a new roof.

hero.headline: South Fork High School freshman describes hot, crowded bus ride on first day of school
hero.teaser: A Martin County parent says her daughter came home in tears after her first bus ride home from South Fork High School, describing extreme heat and overcrowding on the bus Monday.
hero.body:
Sherri Lindemann's daughter is a freshman at South Fork High School. Lindemann said she was caught off guard when she learned what had upset her child. Lindemann said her daughter described a miserable experience on the ride. She said the bus was extremely hot with no air or ventilation and that there was overcrowding with four kids to every seat, with everybody sweaty and upset. The bus ride took an hour and 15 minutes to get home.

The Martin County School District said it understands why the experience would be concerning for students and families, especially on the first day of school when routines are new and students are adjusting to the year ahead. The district's Transportation team confirmed that 57 students were on the bus on Monday, which falls within regulation for high school buses, and that no seat had 4 students in it. Staff also confirmed the bus's air conditioning system was operating properly, but the district acknowledged that mid-August heat can make any bus ride feel particularly warm.

Lindemann's concerns come after the school district consolidated 3 school bus routes to make transportation more efficient without impacting students. In a statement, the district said the delays had nothing to do with the consolidation. The district said Transportation staff are closely monitoring ridership and routes as drivers become more familiar with traffic patterns and students become accustomed to safely exiting the bus. Families can track their child's bus through the MyReaxiumApp. Those who need help setting up an account can contact the transportation department at 772-219-1287.

cards.headline: Troopers seek Ford F-150 driver after deadly e-bike hit-and-run in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: A 48-year-old Vero Beach man riding an electric bicycle was killed after being struck by a pickup truck that fled the scene Sunday night in unincorporated India.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office has located the vehicle allegedly involved in a deadly hit-and-run crash that killed a 48-year-old Vero Beach man riding an electric bicycle Sunday night near 8th Street and 14th Avenue. An IRCSO analyst located a vehicle matching the truck's description, including a missing passenger-side mirror, while reviewing leads with the Florida Highway Patrol. Deputies used Flock Safety technology and other investigative resources to identify the vehicle, its license plate and information about the driver.

The crash occurred at about 8:57 p.m. Sunday when the man was riding an e-bike near 8th Street and 14th Avenue. Investigators said a light-colored Ford F-150, believed to be a 2015 to 2020 model, was traveling behind the man in the same lane. As the pickup approached the bicyclist, the driver took evasive action, traveling southwest and partially entering the eastbound lane. However, the driver was unable to avoid the bicyclist, and the right side of the pickup struck him.

The bicyclist was thrown onto the roadway and came to rest in the eastbound lane of 8th Street. FHP said the driver fled the scene without rendering aid or contacting law enforcement. The bicyclist was taken to Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

The information from IRCSO's Real Time Crime Center allowed FHP to locate the vehicle and confirm its connection to the crash. IRCSO has not identified the driver or released the identity of the bicyclist who was killed.
